newsitem.title: FRANCE: Corsican separatist chief lives dangerously.
newsitem.headline: Corsican separatist chief lives dangerously.

text.p: Francois Santoni, the reclusive but media-wise Corsican separatist leader who turned himself in to French police on Monday, has long known his chosen line of work was a risky one.
Two of his bodyguards have been slain in the past 20 months, one shot dead while sharing his motorcycle, and elite French anti-terror commandos were on his tail.
So Santoni, 36, may breathe a sigh of relief at being safely behind bars as the government cracks down on the movement seeking greater autonomy for the Mediterranean resort island.

The leader of the Cuncolta Naziunalista, the legal front for the hardline Historic Wing of the outlawed Corsican National Liberation Front (FLNC), was sentenced in October to four months in prison for illegally carrying guns.
Since last week, he was also wanted over the bombing of a golf club which refused to pay a four million franc ($800,000) "revolutionary tax" to the FLNC.

Santoni's companion, Cuncolta lawyer Marie-Helene Mattei, was arrested in that case hours before he surrendered to police in Bastia. The golf club owner says it was Mattei who told him on her cellphone to expect the "collectors".
Yet only a few months ago, the government courted Santoni in talks, halfheartedly denied by Paris. Secret emissaries explored a deal to end 20 years of violence on the island.
The high-stakes gamble did not pay off and Prime Minister Alain Juppe called off the talks under parliamentary pressure as bombings continued unabated despite a promised FLNC truce.

Santoni accused Juppe of anti-Corsican racism and warned that a crackdown would "have no effect on the determination to continue a fight which began more than 20 years ago (and which) could even hasten (Juppe's) political demise".

In October, the separatists retaliated for the government's new toughness with the bold bombing of Bordeaux city hall, where Juppe is mayor. After the FLNC claimed responsibility, Santoni found himself a top target.
A furious Juppe, charging that the separatists had chosen "radicalisation" over dialogue, vowed to "dismantle and put out of action" what he referred to as terrorist groups in Corsica.
Santoni, dubbed the "Iguana" by detractors for his reptilian cunning, had apparently hoped after a year as Cuncolta leader to win credit for obtaining a new status for his beloved island.

Instead he found himself spurned by the government, resented by a growing number of Corsicans who polls show are fed up with violence and its economic cost in lost tourism revenue, and threatened with death by rival nationalist movements.
Living in hiding in the Corsican hills, he maintained a high media profile while remaining out of the line of fire of rival separatists eager to settle past scores.

He issued orders and granted press interviews by portable telephone, telling Reuters earlier this year he was not hiding from police but from rival nationalists eager to settle past "vendetta" blood feuds.
